newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish market unmoved by credit, borrowing data.
newsitem.headline: Irish market unmoved by credit, borrowing data.

text.p: Irish financial markets took credit and borrowing data in their stride on Thursday as the focus remained firmly on developments overseas and U.S. March payrolls data in particular, dealers and analysts said.

"I wouldn't expect to see any special impact at all from either of these numbers on the market. It's too much driven right now by the general uncertain external environment in the U.S. and the wider European situation," Dermot O'Brien, chief economist at NCB Stockbrokers, told Reuters.
Earlier, the central bank released monthly statistics showing that private sector Irish credit growth rose by 15.5 percent in February, up from 15.2 percent in January.

But analysts said the data, which was closely watched last year for clues to Irish interest policy, had lost much of its importance following the central bank's annual monetary policy statement in February.

"I get the general impression that it's slipping back into the shadows as a major item for the markets. I think the world has moved on and central bank concerns have moved on and their focus has moved on," NCB's O'Brien said.
"They made that pretty clear in the monetary policy statement. Effectively, in that statement they said we are stuck with tough credit growth and there's not much we can do about it."

Analysts said no clear link had been established between strong credit growth and Irish inflation and the Irish pound exchange rate and the approach of Economic and monetary union were now more important factors for Irish interest rate policy.
Meanwhile, Exchequer Borrowing data, released by the finance ministry this afternoon, confirmed the strength of the Irish economy but was unlikely to have any market impact, analysts said.
The EBR totalled 151 million Irish pounds in the first quarter, well below the 561 million seen at the same time last year, but the figures were flattered by timing factors.
By 1615 GMT, 10-year Irish bonds were at 107.00 to yield 6.95 percent against 107.05 before the data while five-year paper was broadly unchanged at 101.00 to yield 6.23.
On the money market, one-month money was unchanged at 5.63/5.75 percent.

Analysts said attention was focused on U.S. March non-farm payrolls, due for release at 1330 GMT on Friday, as international markets seek clues to the likelihood of further rate hikes by the U.S. Federal Reserve.
